children.value: A radio station must report every song it played, and the presenter often talks over the beginning and the end of a song. A music fan who holds a phone towards a loudspeaker in a noisy bar has the same problem: identify one exact recording among millions from a few seconds of distorted sound, within a second. Features that describe how music sounds return similar songs, not the one recording. Comparing waveforms or spectra fails as well, because the noise changes every sample and every spectral value (

solves the problem with a different kind of feature. It does not describe the sound for similarity, nor classify it into labels. It extracts a compact set of codes, the fingerprint, from the parts of the signal that survive noise, and looks these codes up in a hash index of all catalogued recordings. This section follows the method that Wang (2003) published for Shazam in five steps: spectrogram, constellation map, combinatorial hashing, query fingerprint, and matching with an offset histogram. A small experiment with four public music recordings carries the numbers through all steps.
The first step computes a spectrogram, as in
(left) shows one for a pop song. Noise spreads its energy over many frequencies and frames, while the instruments and voices of the song concentrate their energy in strong, localized peaks.

The second step keeps only these peaks. A point of the spectrogram becomes a peak if its energy is the maximum within a neighborhood of frequency bins and frames, and above a minimum level. The result is the
, a sparse set of points in the time-frequency plane (
, right), named after its resemblance to a star chart. Everything else is discarded: the amplitudes, the phases, and the weaker parts of the spectrum.

The peaks are robust for three reasons. Background noise adds energy, but rarely enough to displace the strongest peak in a neighborhood. Compression and the coloring of a phone microphone change the amplitudes of frequency bands, but not the positions of their maxima. And the method needs only a fraction of the peaks to survive, as the matching step will show.

The catalogue of the experiment holds four public recordings: the Brahms clip played by a string orchestra (45.8 s), Tchaikovsky’s Dance of the Sugar Plum Fairy (119.9 s), the jazz piece Vibe Ace (61.5 s), and a trumpet loop (5.3 s), all resampled to 11,025 Hz. The spectrogram uses frames of 1024 samples (93 ms) with a hop of 256 samples (23.2 ms). A peak must be the maximum in a neighborhood of 15 bins by 15 frames, that is, about 160 Hz by 350 ms, and lie less than 50 dB below the strongest point of the recording. The 45.8-second Brahms clip yields 2,317 peaks, about 50 per second.

A single peak is a weak fingerprint. Its frequency bin takes one of 513 values, so a query peak matches thousands of peaks in a large catalogue by chance. The third step therefore combines peaks into pairs. Each peak serves as an
is defined in front of it: a time window after the anchor and a frequency range around it. The anchor is paired with peaks inside its target zone (
), and each pair is encoded as a hash of three values:

The pair is far more specific than a single peak, since three values must match instead of one. It contains no absolute time, only the distance between the two peaks, so the same pair produces the same hash wherever the query starts in the recording. And the redundancy makes it robust: each peak takes part in several pairs, so a peak lost to noise destroys only its own pairs, while a peak added by noise creates pairs that exist nowhere in the catalogue and simply find no match.

The hashes of all catalogued recordings form an inverted file, the index structure of text search: the hash plays the role of the term, and its postings list holds the recordings and anchor times in which it occurs (

Each anchor is paired with at most 5 peaks that lie between 1 and 64 frames (23 ms to 1.5 s) after it and within 64 bins (690 Hz) above or below it. The Brahms clip yields 11,471 hashes, about five per peak, and the catalogue of four recordings yields 55,125 postings under 45,751 distinct hashes. With 513 anchor bins, up to 129 target bins, and 64 time distances, there are about 4.2 million possible hashes, so most hashes occur only once or a few times.

The fourth step processes the query exactly like the catalogue: spectrogram, peaks, pairs, and hashes. The fifth step looks up every query hash in the index. Many lookups return matches, most of them by chance, because the same pair of frequencies and distance also occurs somewhere in other recordings. The decisive test is the time. Example: the presenter talks over the music

The query is a 10-second excerpt of the Brahms clip that starts at 20.0 seconds. In the hard version, a LibriVox reading is mixed in at the same energy as the music (0 dB), as when a presenter speaks over a song, and the mixture is limited to the telephone band of 300 to 3400 Hz.

In both cases, Brahms wins, and the offset of 19.99 s (861 frames of 23.2 ms) recovers the position of the excerpt. The voice destroys most hashes of the music, but 201 still agree on the offset, against 3 for the best wrong recording. The histogram makes the difference: counting matched hashes alone gives a ratio of 286 to 174 between Brahms and Tchaikovsky, the alignment check a ratio of 201 to 3. The 120-second Tchaikovsky clip collects many chance matches because it is long, but they spread over 167 different offsets. With the voice 5 dB louder than the music, Brahms still gets 130 aligned votes.

Even the clean excerpt agrees on the offset with only 768 of its 2,182 hashes. The excerpt starts at sample 220,500, which is 861.3 frames, so its frames are shifted by a third of a hop against those of the catalogue. Some peaks move to a neighboring bin or frame, and their hashes change.

The lookup is fast because it never compares the query with the recordings themselves. Each query hash costs one access to the hash index and a pass over a short postings list; the histograms only count the matched entries. The work grows with the number of matched postings, not with the duration of the catalogue, which is how the same method answers within a second for catalogues of millions of recordings.

This specialization has a price: the fingerprint matches recordings, not songs. A live performance, a cover version, or someone singing the melody produce different peaks, and the hashes no longer match. Changes of pitch and speed hurt as well: a pitch shift moves all frequencies, and a speed change stretches all time distances. On the clean 10-second Brahms excerpt, half a semitone higher leaves 1 aligned vote instead of 768, fewer than the 3 of a wrong recording. A speed change is less severe, because the short time distances of many pairs change by less than one frame: 2% faster still gives 94 votes, 5% faster 30. Robust variants quantize the hash values more coarsely or search over several stretch factors, at the cost of more chance matches.

Within these limits, fingerprinting serves several tasks beyond naming songs for listeners. Broadcast monitoring services compare the program of radio and television stations with a catalogue to produce the play lists for royalty reports, the radio station’s problem. Upload platforms match new videos against the fingerprints of copyrighted material. Archives find duplicate recordings that were digitized several times from different tapes.

Build constellation maps, test which peaks survive added noise, generate pair hashes, identify a noisy query with offset histograms, measure the effect of pitch and speed changes, and write the play list of a short broadcast.
